name: Jefferson curl

lead: The Jefferson curl has you slowly roll the spine into flexion while holding a light weight, then return to standing. It is discussed in strength, rehabilitation and posture communities as a way to build hamstring and back flexibility and posterior-chain tolerance.

Proponents say gradual loaded flexion through a controlled range increases flexibility and conditions the spine's tissues. A 2026 cross-sectional EMG study in resistance-trained adults compared erector spinae activation with a Romanian deadlift and described the exercise as popular but lacking empirical characterisation; no trial tests it for posture or appearance.

paras: People do it slowly with a light load, one vertebra at a time, as a mobility or accessory exercise in strength programs, progressing weight gradually over weeks.

Loaded spinal flexion is a movement pattern that some clinicians and coaches advise caution with, particularly for people with back pain. A qualitative study found people with chronic low back pain perceiving some exercises as potentially injurious. No injury-rate data specific to the Jefferson curl were found.

angle.text: Popular in strength circles as a mobility exercise for the spine and hamstrings, sometimes tied to better flexibility and back posture. One small 2026 EMG study has measured muscle activity; its appearance use is based on user accounts.

lead: The Jefferson curl is a loaded spinal flexion exercise: standing on a box or the floor with a light weight, the lifter slowly curls the spine forward and down, one segment at a time, then reverses the movement back to standing.[1] People use it to build hamstring and spinal flexibility and to condition the muscles along the back of the body, which they link to a stronger-looking back, better movement and a more upright carriage.

A 2026 paper describes the exercise as having gained popularity in strength and rehabilitation practice while lacking empirical characterisation.[1] The study, a cross-sectional surface electromyography (EMG) comparison in resistance-trained adults, examined erector spinae activation during the Jefferson curl against a Romanian deadlift at a matched submaximal load.[1]

On T Nation, lifters discuss the movement alongside stiff-legged deadlifts and weighted forward bends, and debate whether loading the spine in flexion is acceptable, citing coaches and clinicians with differing views.[2][3][4]

paras: Unlike a hip hinge, where the spine is held roughly neutral, the Jefferson curl intentionally takes the spine through flexion under load. It is typically performed slowly with a light weight and, according to proponents, aims at hamstring and spinal mobility and tolerance of flexed positions.[1]

A T Nation training log from 2023 describes it as a forward bend or toe touch with weights and rounding of the lower back, and mentions a coaching progression that advises capping the load at 100 lb.[2]

A 2026 cross-sectional study in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy used surface EMG in resistance-trained adults to characterise erector spinae activation during the Jefferson curl at a load matched to the Romanian deadlift, testing whether the two exercises differ at the same absolute load.[1] It measured muscle activation and did not assess long-term mobility, posture, injury or appearance outcomes.

No trials found test the Jefferson curl for posture, flexibility gains or back-pain outcomes. A 2026 exploratory study of breakdancers examined anthropometric and neuromuscular characteristics across performance levels and is related only to flexibility-oriented training in general.[5]

Loaded spinal flexion is a movement pattern that some coaches and clinicians treat cautiously. On T Nation, posters cite spine researcher Stuart McGill and others as cautioning against repeated flexion under load, while others argue that exposure to spinal movement under light load is reasonable.[3][4][6]

No data specific to the Jefferson curl on injury rates were found. A 2025 qualitative study of people with chronic low back pain reported that participants, without clinical guidance, sometimes perceived certain exercises as risky, with one participant saying they could see themselves getting hurt if they did it wrong. This concerns exercise perception in general rather than this movement.[7]

lore.intro: On T Nation, the Jefferson curl comes up in training logs and in recurring debates about whether spinal flexion under load is acceptable.[2][3][4]

claims.claim: Loaded spinal flexion is risky and should be avoided
Light loaded flexion is useful exposure for the spine
The exercise is comparable to the Romanian deadlift for the back muscles
